name: Hu tieu My Tho
summary: A rice-noodle bowl from Mỹ Tho, eaten dry or with broth at breakfast, lunch, or supper. The strand is tied to Gò Cát rice. The national page says it is not hủ tiếu Tàu, hủ tiếu Nam Vang, phở, or bún bò Huế. A stall price is check on arrival.
origin: Mỹ Tho. The strand is tied to fragrant Gò Cát rice grown in phường Mỹ Phong.
history: The provincial tourism article says the bowl appears at the start of the 1960s, from carts between Mỹ Tho and Gò Công, and that in 2014 it was recognized as a dish of Asian culinary value. The national page also starts the fame in the 1960s and names the cooks Phánh Ký, Tuyền Ký, and Nam Sơn.

The city portal says the dish has a hundred years of cultural value, that a cooperative and the village formed in 2007, and that in December 2008 the Intellectual Property Office granted a certificate for the brand Hủ tiếu Mỹ Tho. That longer line sits beside the 1960s account. A ward-page ranking is not part of the story.
culture: The old phường 9 page says the bowl is used for all three meals. The national page says the Mỹ Tho bowl is not the same as hủ tiếu Tàu, hủ tiếu Nam Vang, phở, or bún bò Huế, and that the local way uses fresh bean sprouts, lime, chili, and soy.
The workshop is ấp Hội Gia, phường Mỹ Phong, where you watch the sheets. The bowl itself is in town and at the pier court. Gò Công’s kiln is not a Mỹ Tho stall.
texture: The provincial tourism article says a good strand smells of rice, stays soft without going mushy, and is not sour. The ward page says the strands are blanched briefly. Too long and they go soft.
taste: The ward page sets the table with soy, lime, sugar, and fresh chili or satay, mixed by the guest. It does not name one flavor for the broth.
Two broth lists stay side by side. The provincial article: pork leg bone, grilled dried squid, cassava root, and spices, kept at a simmer. The ward page: bone, dried squid, dried shrimp, and daikon.
howToEat: Order it dry, or with the broth poured over. Dry, the ward page says the strands are tossed with pork crackling, fried shallot, and soy, then topped with cooked minced pork. The soup style adds sliced pork, liver, intestines, shrimp, squid, and quail egg, then the broth, spring onion, and more crackling.
The national page says the bowl is not eaten with lettuce, vinegar, and a herb plate. The ward page still puts spring onion on the soup. Blanch the strands briefly.
A stall price was not copied. The price is check on arrival.
where: Town streets, and the pier food court on đường 30 Tháng 4. A 5 Jan 2019 article prints that court as 18:30–02:00. A travel page prints a night market at số 8 đường 30/4 from 18:00, busiest 19:00–22:00. Confirm which clock still holds.

Ấp Hội Gia is the workshop, open 07:00–18:00 on the portal, not the place the bowl is served. The last line of the fame is Mỹ Tho. Hủ tiếu Sa Đéc and hủ tiếu Nam Vang are other bowls, and they have no pages here.
seoTitle: Hu tieu My Tho — dry or with broth
seoDescription: The Mỹ Tho rice-noodle bowl, dry or with broth, at any meal. Gò Cát rice, two broth lists, and a stall price that is check on arrival.
